 Charles Bronson told the parole board at an earlier hearing he had ‘had more porridge than Goldilocks and the Three Bears’
 Credit : Shutterstock/Lindsey Parnaby
 Telegraph Reporters
 Published 
 17 November 2026 3:42pm GMT
 Charles Bronson, one of the UK’s longest-serving inmates, has again been refused release after his ninth parole hearing .
 The hearing for Bronson, whose real name is Michael Peterson, took place in private earlier this month.
 His eighth hearing in 2023 was Britain’s second to be held in public.
 Bronson has spent most of the past five decades in jail – bar two brief periods during which he reoffended. This has included 11 hostage-taking incidents in nine different sieges, with victims including prison governors, doctors, staff and, on one occasion, his own solicitor.
 Bronson was first convicted in 1974 when he was 21 and was jailed for seven years for robbery, aggravated burglary, assault with intent to rob and possession of a firearm.
 He has spent most of his life in prison for a string of different offences, and was handed a discretionary life sentence with a minimum term of four years in 2000 for taking a prison teacher at HMP Hull hostage for 44 hours.
 The long-serving prisoner, who has been diagnosed with anti-social personality disorder, has been repeatedly turned down for release .
 Earlier this year he applied for his latest parole hearing to be held in public, but was turned down on the grounds that there were not the resources to do so.
 After release from prison in 1987 Charles Bronson took up a brief career in bare-knuckle boxing
 Credit : Enterprise News
 Jeremy Roberts KC, a parole board member, said he was prepared to believe that Bronson’s intentions in applying for another public hearing were “entirely genuine even if (as is likely) there is an element of attention-seeking in his application”.
 Bronson, who changed his surname to Salvador in 2014, gave evidence at length at his previous parole hearing, telling the panel that he dreamt of walking barefoot on grass, and wanted his elderly mother to see him released before she died.
 He said: “It’s no secret I have had more porridge than Goldilocks and the Three Bears, and I’m sick of it. I’ve had enough of it: I want to go home.”
 The 73-year-old chose not to attend his latest hearing earlier this month, but told the panel through his lawyer that he accepted he would not be released or moved to open conditions.
 Charles Bronson has convictions for 11 hostage-taking incidents during nine different sieges
 Credit : Nick Razzell
 In its decision, published on Tuesday, the parole board panel found that “Mr Salvador continued to find it hard to trust people in authority”.
 It continued: “The panel learned that his behaviour had continued to be mixed since his last review.
 “There were some positive reports about Mr Salvador including in relation to his engagement with staff and insight into his past use of violence.
 “There had however also been further incidents of violence against staff and other prisoners.
 “The evidence provided also indicated that Mr Salvador lacked the motivation to abide by prison rules.”

 Three members of staff responsible for Bronson gave spoken testimony but none supported release, nor did those who wrote reports including a prison psychologist.
 The panel said: “After considering the circumstances of Mr Salvador’s offending, his behaviour, the limited progress made while in custody and all the other evidence presented at the hearing and in the dossier, the panel was not satisfied that his release at this point would be safe for the protection of the public.
 “Nor did the panel recommend to the Secretary of State that Mr Salvador should be transferred to open prison.”
